cues.text: The one-line summary.
Every later lesson — precision, shapes, sharding — leans on one word: tensor.
It sounds exotic.
It isn't.
To the hardware, a tensor is just a multidimensional array of numbers — a flat row of values in memory, plus a shape that says how to read them.
A single number, a list, a grid, a cube of numbers: all tensors, differing only in how many dimensions they have.
Get that, and "the model is just tensors flowing through chips" stops being a slogan and becomes something you can reason about.
Infra bridge.
You already think this way.
A config value is one number.
A time series is a list.
A routing table is a grid.
Stack routing tables across VRFs and you've got a cube.
Those are ranks 0, 1, 2, 3 — the only thing that changes is how many indices you need to reach one value.
Run it yourself.
A short Colab notebook reads a tensor's rank and shape straight off numpy, then computes the footprint and charts the rank → memory blow-up (watch rank 3 punch through a chip's HBM).
Pure numpy, runs on CPU, no GPU.
From an arrow to an array — the shadow trick.
So where do the numbers come from?
Start with something physical: an arrow in space (a direction with a length).
You can't store an arrow — but you can measure its shadow on each axis.
Those shadow lengths are the arrow's components, and that list of components — [x, y, z] — is the array the computer keeps.
Drag the arrow below and watch geometry turn into a stored array:

The shadow on an axis is called a projection; the little length-1 rulers (x̂, ŷ, ẑ — the caret ˆ just means "length exactly 1 along that axis") are the basis vectors, the agreed unit that makes the numbers mean a real direction.
Infra bridge.
This is serialization.
The arrow is the rich object; the components are the wire format — a flat list both sides agree how to read.
The basis vectors are the protocol: sender and receiver agree the first number means "along x," and the integers suddenly mean something.
The chip only ever ships the flat list.

You'll essentially never touch basis vectors operating ML systems — but they're why a flat list of numbers can stand in for a real object, which is the same reason a wrong shape, not a wrong value, is what usually breaks a run.
Rank — how many dimensions.
The one number that classifies a tensor is its rank: how many dimensions it has, i.e. how many indices you need to reach a single value.
rank 0 — a scalar, one number, shape ().
rank 1 — a vector, a list, shape (n,) — the [x, y, z] above.
rank 2 — a matrix, a grid, shape (rows, cols).
rank 3+ — a cube and beyond, like [batch, seq, hidden].
One naming trap.
"Rank" here means number of dimensions (you'll also see ndim or order).
It is not the linear-algebra "rank of a matrix" (the count of independent rows).
Same word, unrelated idea — when an ML tool says a tensor is "rank 3," it means three axes.
A tensor you already know — a digital image.
Forget arrows for a second.
A digital image is a tensor, and it shows you every rank at once:
A grayscale photo is literally a grid of brightness numbers — one per pixel.
Now make it color: you don't get a new picture, you get a third dimension — a new axis called channels.
The same grid, but three values deep — how much red, green, and blue sit at each pixel.
That channels axis is exactly the jump from a matrix to a rank-3 tensor.
Stack a batch of photos (or a video's frames) and you've added a fourth.
Walk an image up the ranks yourself — one pixel, a row, a grayscale grid, then color (the +RGB channels dimension), then a stack of frames — and watch the stored array grow right alongside it:
Infra bridge.
That 4K screenshot you just scp'd is a rank-3 tensor — 3840 × 2160 × 3 bytes ≈ 24 MB uncompressed.
The file size is the shape times the bytes-per-value.
Going grayscale → color tripled it (one extra dimension, ×3); a batch multiplies again.
It's the same arithmetic as the memory table below — and the same reason video and image models are so HBM-hungry.
Step through the ranks and watch the structure grow:
Why rank is the scariest word in a memory budget.
Here's the operational punchline.
Each dimension you add doesn't add to the size — it multiplies it.
The number of elements is the product of the dimensions, so growth is multiplicative, not additive.
Make it concrete at model scale — every dimension 4096 wide, in bf16 (2 bytes each):
One extra dimension took the same kind of data from 32 MiB to 128 GiB — past a single accelerator's HBM (today's high-end parts hold ~80–140 GB).
Nothing changed but the rank.
Infra bridge.
This is why "just add a dimension" terrifies the people sizing the cluster.

Activations (the chip's intermediate scratch values for each layer) and the KV-cache (a per-token scratchpad attention keeps in HBM to avoid recomputing earlier tokens) both carry batch and sequence and hidden dimensions — every one a multiplier.
When a job OOMs on a longer context or a bigger batch, you're watching this table play out — HBM utilization climbs until the run dies.
The element count, not the dtype, is usually the culprit.
Where the word comes from (optional, and lovely).
If you want the deeper geometric story — why we even say "tensor," and how basis vectors carry it — Dan Fleisch explains it in twelve minutes with blocks and a desk lamp.
It's the physics view (which adds coordinate-system machinery we don't need to operate chips), but it's the clearest intuition for the shadow trick you used above.
For operating ML systems, the array definition is all you need: a tensor is a multidimensional array, and its rank is how many dimensions it has.
Why this matters.
It's the vocabulary for everything else.
Shapes, padding, precision, sharding — all of it is.
"what's the rank and the shape, and how many bytes does that come to."
Rank drives the memory bill.
Sizing HBM, predicting an OOM, reading why a longer sequence.
blows up — all start with "how many dimensions, each how big, times the dtype."
The chip stores a flat array.
No arrows, no geometry at runtime — just a row of numbers and a.
shape.
That's why a wrong shape, not a wrong value, is what usually breaks a run — and the next lesson, on tensor shapes, shows how to compute that footprint before a job ever starts.
